item.title: Chemistry Seminar Presented by Prof. Hans Renata (Rice University)Combining Synthetic Chemistry and Biology to Streamline Access to Complex Molecules — Tue Dec 1, 11:40 AM — French Family Science Center 2237
item.description: The Department of Chemistry is excited to host Prof. Hans Renata (Rice University) on Tuesday, December 1, 2026, for a departmental seminar. By virtue of their unrivaled selectivity profiles, enzymes possess remarkable potential to address unsolved challenges in chemical synthesis. The realization of this potential, however, has only recently gained traction. Recent advances in enzyme engineering and genome mining have provided a powerful platform for identifying and optimizing enzymatic transformations for synthetic applications and allowed us to begin formulating novel synthetic strategies and disconnections. This talk will describe our recent efforts in developing a new design language in chemical synthesis that centers on the incorporation of biocatalytic approaches in contemporary synthetic logic. Case studies will focus on the use of this platform in the chemoenzymatic syntheses of complex natural products. To learn more about Prof. Hans Renata (Rice University) research, please

item.title: Project RESTORE Educator Trek: Waterdog Warriors — Sat Dec 5, 9:00 AM — North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Date: Saturday, December 5, 2026. Please also mark your calendar for a rain date on Sunday, December 6! Times: 9am to 5pm
Join us in the search for one of North Carolina’s rarest salamanders, the federally threatened Neuse River waterdog, found only in the Neuse and Tar-Pamlico River Basins in North Carolina. Learn from expert biologists, explore the natural history of the waterdog, observe historically collected specimens and participate in field monitoring of the species. Discover how you can bring the excitement of field research of this rare species into your classroom.
With support from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Project RESTORE (Rescuing Endangered Species Through Outreach, Restoration, and Education) will feature a suite of educational opportunities for teachers and students to participate in restoration and monitoring of imperiled and endangered species in eastern North Carolina.

item.title: Pursuing Qualitative Grant Funding — Fri Feb 5, 9:00 AM
item.description:
Securing funding is one of the most consequential — and least openly discussed — dimensions of a research career. For scholars whose work centers social inequality and structurally marginalized communities, pursuing funding carries unique political and institutional complexities. This workshop engages those realities directly. Participants will examine how funding priorities are shaped, how research agendas can be both advanced and constrained by funders, and how to build a diversified, sustainable funding strategy across sectors — without losing sight of their scholarly mission or community commitments.
In this workshop, Dr. Rashawn Ray, whose funding portfolio spans federal agencies, private foundations, and philanthropic institutions, will demystify the landscape of public and private research support. item.title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math — Mon Feb 22
item.description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.
Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. item.description:
The Sperling Center for Jewish Studies at Duke University is pleased to present its Undergraduate Documentary Film Festival, featuring original documentary films created by Duke undergraduates exploring Jewish history, culture, religion, memory, and contemporary Jewish life.
Drawing on archival research, oral histories, interviews, and personal narratives, student filmmakers bring Jewish Studies scholarship to life through the medium of film. This year's projects explore the history and contemporary experiences of Morocco's Sephardic Jewish community and the complex dynamics of Jewish-Muslim relations, as well as the story of the family of Keith Siegel, who was taken hostage during the October 7 attacks. Through these films, students examine questions of identity, memory, resilience, intercommunal relations, and the ways global events resonate within local communities, including at Duke and in Durham.
